newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Slovak c.bank policy tough but realistic-analysts.
newsitem.headline: Slovak c.bank policy tough but realistic-analysts.

text.p: The National Bank of Slovakia's (NBS) 1997 monetary policy may be tough on the fledgling economy, but is realistic overall, analysts said on Thursday.
NBS Governor Vladimir Masar announced next year's policy to a news conference, forecasting GDP growth to slow to five percent, year-on-year, from an expected six percent this year.

"We expect an easing of real GDP growth to five percent (in 1997)," Masar said. "Such growth would be favourable, but also maintainable with regard to the potential of the economy and...stability of the environment."
Masar said inflation in 1997 should hold steady at 4.9 to 5.7 percent, while growth in the money supply, a constant problem for the central bank, should ease to a year-on-year rate of 10.7 percent.

Analysts said the targets were achievable, but may come at a considerable cost to the economy. "The planned targets may be a bit optimistic but still realistic, except for M2 growth," Vladimir Kuklis of CSOB bank told Reuters.
He said the plan to keep money supply growth so low could negatively affect the current lack of investment, seen as one of the most serious problems faced by the Slovak economy.
"At this moment, it seems too cruel for the entire economy, which is dramatically undercapitalised," Kuklis said.

Masar said the NBS expected domestic sources to continue having the strongest impact on M2 in the next year though Kuklis countered that the economy's need for investment may outweigh the risk of inflation.

Earlier on Thursday, the Slovak Statistics Bureau (SUSR) released statistics showing the economy continued its strong performance in the third quarter, with year-on-year GDP growth of 7.0 percent while inflation held at 5.4 percent in November.
SUSR also said that full year 1996 GDP should rise by between 6.8-7.0 percent, while inflation will remain under six percent.

"If GDP growth slows down through tight monetary policies then the risk of an overheating economy would definitely decrease, and lower inflation could also be expected," Jozef Gasparik, an analyst at Creditanstalt, said.
"This year's figures can be called a success. However, I would probably estimate next year's inflation a bit higher, to allow a cushion for elements such as higher energy prices," he added.
